title: Climbing Aconcagua: Full Guide
excerpt: Aconcagua, 6,962 m, is the highest mountain outside Asia. The full guide: the Normal Route, high camps, permit, season, acclimatization and what the summit takes.
seoTitle: Climbing Aconcagua: Normal Route Guide, Permit, Season and Cost

content.value: On day 15 of the expedition, from Camp 3 at 5,970 m, climbers set out on their longest day: the ascent to the summit of Aconcagua, 6,962 m (22,841 ft), the highest point in the Americas and in the whole world outside Asia, and the descent back to the tents. Reaching that day takes about three weeks in Argentina, previous experience at altitude, a climbing permit from Aconcagua Provincial Park and a patient acclimatization schedule. The Normal Route requires no technical climbing, but the altitude, the cold and the wind make it a genuine mountaineering expedition.

Trip reports from Aconcagua are easy to find. An orderly picture of what it actually takes is harder. This guide puts things in order: what makes the mountain hard, how the Normal Route works camp by camp, what the permit costs and requires, when the season is, and how our expedition looks day by day. If Kilimanjaro or a high-altitude trek is already behind you and you are asking what comes next, this is where to start.
Why Aconcagua is harder than it looks

Aconcagua rises in the Andes, entirely within Argentina, in Mendoza Province. It is the highest mountain in the Americas and the highest in the world outside Asia. It is one of the Seven Summits, the highest points on each continent, and thousands of climbers attempt it every season.

On paper it is a mountain without technical sections: on the Normal Route there are no rock or ice walls and no need for ropes. That is exactly why it misleads. Aconcagua is not a "trekking peak": acute mountain sickness, and in serious cases high-altitude pulmonary and cerebral edema, are seen on the mountain regularly. Changeable weather, strong wind, cold and lack of oxygen, together with the inexperience of some climbers, raise the real difficulty far beyond what the map suggests.

content.title: ✦ The wind decides
content.value: The winds high on Aconcagua sometimes exceed 100 km/h and can destroy an entire camp above 6,000 m. Days like that close the summit, which is why the itinerary has to leave room for waiting.

The cold is part of the equation too: the wind chill on summit day can reach minus 30°C (minus 22°F) or lower, so the gear you need is that of a mountain above 7,000 m. The climate is dry: moisture from the Pacific falls mostly on the Chilean side of the Andes and crosses to the Argentine side as a warm, dry wind called the Zonda. On clear days at base camp it is actually hot, and you need to drink a lot. On the same expedition you deal with desert sun and with the cold of very high mountains.
The Normal Route, camp by camp

Aconcagua has several routes, from the famous South Face to the Polish Glacier, but most climbers use one of two. The first is the Normal Route, which enters the park through the Horcones Valley and passes the Plaza de Mulas base camp. The second is the 360 Route, which enters through the Vacas Valley, passes the Plaza Argentina base camp and joins the Normal Route at Cólera camp, from where the way to the summit is shared. Both have similar technical difficulty. The HighAir expedition climbs the Normal Route.
Mendoza, Puente del Inca and Confluencia

The journey starts in Mendoza, at 760 m, a city whose metropolitan area has about one million inhabitants and hospitals of every level, in a region famous for its wines. From there you drive west on international highway No. 7 to the villages at the foot of the mountain, among them Puente del Inca at 2,700 m. The park entrance, in the Horcones Valley, lies about 190 km west of Mendoza. After the permit check at the ranger station, a walk of 3 to 4 hours leads to Confluencia, the first camp, at 3,400 m.

At Confluencia you register with the park rangers and undergo the first medical check inside the park, which is mandatory. It includes a questionnaire on previous experience, training and medication, measurement of blood oxygen saturation, pulse and blood pressure, and listening to the lungs. Anyone who does not pass the medical checks does not continue.

content.value: Plaza de Mulas: base camp

From Confluencia a long walk continues to Plaza de Mulas, the base camp of the Normal Route, at 4,300 m. Personal gear comes up here on mules. In the busy season the camp becomes a small mountain village: service companies run dining tents, showers and internet, and a medical team, park rangers and the Mendoza Police rescue patrol work there. Here too every climber has a medical check and registers at the ranger station before going higher. On our expedition base camp is home for six nights: you leave it for acclimatization walks, carry gear from it to the first camp, and come back to it to rest.
Three high camps

Above base camp there are three high camps. In our itinerary they are called Camp 1 (5,050 m), Camp 2 (5,550 m) and Camp 3 (5,970 m), and on the mountain they are known as Canadá, Nido de Cóndores and Cólera. Nido de Cóndores sits on wide, flat ground, and it is the last helicopter evacuation point. Many climbers spend more than one night there, because it is the last chance to acclimatize before the upper mountain. Cólera is the most used Camp 3, and 10 to 15 minutes away is the older Berlin camp.
Summit day: Independencia, the Traverse and the Canaleta

Summit day falls into three sections. The first is a steep climb of about 3 hours from Camp 3 to Independencia, the ruins of an old wooden hut at almost 6,400 m. From there progress slows, wind and cold are strongly felt, and this is also where many who feel unwell decide to turn back. The second section, the Traverse, is a wind-exposed crossing of two to three hours to La Cueva, "the Cave", at 6,700 m. The third is the Canaleta, a steep gully that climbs from the Cave to the summit in two to three hours, and it is the hardest physically and mentally. Most of the time snow and ice on the upper mountain mean putting on crampons from Independencia.

Such a day lasts about 13 to 14 hours up and down, and most climbers sleep at Camp 3 again afterwards. The summit is only halfway: most incidents on Aconcagua happen on the descent, so it is important to reach the top with enough strength and time in hand to come down safely. Our itinerary is built the same way, returning to sleep at Camp 3 after the summit and descending to base camp only the next day.

content.value: Our expedition, day by day
The HighAir Aconcagua expedition lasts 20 days, from landing in Mendoza to the flight home, and about 17 of them are spent inside the park. This is the itinerary:

items: Day 1: arrival in Mendoza (760 m) and preparation.
Day 2: drive to Puente del Inca (2,700 m).
Day 3: entry to the park in the Horcones Valley and walk to Confluencia (3,400 m).
Day 4: acclimatization day, walk to Plaza Francia (4,000 m) and back to Confluencia.
Day 5: ascent to Plaza de Mulas, base camp (4,300 m).
Day 7: ascent of Cerro Bonete (5,000 m) and back to base camp.
Day 9: gear carry to Camp 1 (5,050 m) and back to base camp.
Day 15: summit day (6,962 m) and back to Camp 3.
Days 16 and 17: buffer days in case of bad weather.
Day 18: descent from Camp 3 to base camp.
Day 19: exit from the park, via Puente del Inca, and back to Mendoza.
Day 20: transfer to the airport and flight home.

content.value: Two principles guide the itinerary. The first is "climb high, sleep low": on day 4 you climb to Plaza Francia and come back to sleep at Confluencia, and on days 7 and 9 you climb Cerro Bonete and to Camp 1 and descend to sleep at base camp. That way the body meets 5,000 m several days before it sleeps there. The second principle is patience: a rest day after every big effort, and an extra night at Camp 2 before the final climb.

content.title: ✦ Two days for the weather
content.value: Our itinerary has two buffer days, days 16 and 17, set aside for bad weather. If the wind closes the summit on the planned day, the group can wait for a better window without giving up the summit attempt in advance.
Climbing permit, insurance and documents

Everyone who climbs Aconcagua needs a climbing permit from the provincial park. The price is set anew every season, and it depends on the route and on whether you climb with an authorized service company. In the 2025/26 season a foreign climber with an authorized company paid 1,170 US dollars on the Horcones route, and in the early sale for the 2026/27 season the same permit was offered at 950 dollars.
The price is set in dollars and paid in Argentine pesos. The climbing permit is not included in the price of our expedition, and we help you obtain it.

Everyone entering the park to climb must have insurance covering search, rescue and evacuation. Make sure the policy is in English or Spanish, carries an identifying policy number and explicitly covers helicopter evacuation. Insurance is not included in the price of the expedition.

The permit is issued through an authorized local service company, which registers the climber and the expedition. This requires, among other things, a passport, an expedition form, a risk acceptance declaration, proof of payment and proof of insurance. On our side, an extended medical clearance including an ECG and blood tests, and a health declaration, are conditions for departure. Citizens of the US, Canada, the UK, the EU and most of Latin America enter Argentina without a visa for a tourist stay. Check the validity of your passport and the current entry rules for your nationality before you fly.
When to climb Aconcagua

Aconcagua lies in the southern hemisphere, so the climbing season is the summer there. In the official season, roughly from early December to early March, rangers, a medical service and helicopters operate on the mountain. Season dates change slightly from year to year, and outside the season climbing is allowed only with a special winter permit, with no services inside the park. Our expeditions depart between December and February, in the heart of the season.

content.value: Who it suits

Aconcagua is not a first mountain. We require previous experience at an altitude of at least 5,000 m, for example a Kilimanjaro climb (5,895 m) or the Everest Base Camp trek, which reaches Kala Patthar (5,545 m). Beyond the altitude itself, that experience teaches you how your body reacts to lack of oxygen, to cold and to long days. In terms of fitness, anyone who can walk about 20 km a day, enjoys a challenge and is highly motivated has a good starting point, and the rest is built with a structured training plan before departure. We wrote about the order in which climbers usually progress from mountain to mountain in our Seven Summits guide.

Personal gear is part of safety. High mountain boots and warm down clothing are essential, and we also require a sleeping bag rated to minus 25°C (minus 13°F). Every registered climber receives a detailed gear list and a training plan for the climb, a personal gear checklist with an online gear consultation, and an online preparation call with the group and the guide.

Good to know: the climb is led by professional local guides who speak English and Spanish and have long experience leading groups on the mountain. Basic English or Spanish, enough to follow instructions on the trail, is worth having. Following the instructions of the crew is mandatory, and the route may change according to the weather and the judgment of the guides. In the mountains there is no promise of a summit, only a commitment to safety.
Aconcagua with HighAir

Our Aconcagua expedition lasts 20 days, departs in the season between December and February, and is limited to 9 participants. The price is 10,000 US dollars per person, and the success rate we publish on the mountain is 75 percent.

The price includes airport transfers to the hotel in Mendoza and back, internal transfers to the start of the route and back, 2 nights in a 5-star hotel in Mendoza with breakfast, a night at a hotel in Puente del Inca with breakfast, single tents during the climb, tent setup and takedown at the three high camps, three full meals a day throughout the climb, professional local English- and Spanish-speaking guides, mules to carry up to 35 kg of personal gear per person to base camp, a personal porter to carry up to 20 kg of gear at the high camps, showers and toilets at base camp, Wi-Fi and charging stations at the camps, a Magnus satellite device for the group, help obtaining the climbing permits, a first aid kit with emergency oxygen cylinders, a personal area in the HighAir app, a detailed gear list and a training plan for the climb, an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide before departure, support with flight and travel insurance questions before departure, a gift kit with a cap, a dry-fit shirt and a 100-liter duffel bag, and a meaningful donation to the fight against cancer.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance with evacuation cover (required), lunch and dinner at the hotels in Mendoza and Puente del Inca, personal gear (clothing, footwear, climbing gear and summit boots), tips for the guides, the climbing permit fee (1,000 to 1,300 dollars per person), additional porters beyond the 20 kg included in the program, an extra hotel night if needed, and personal expenses such as drinks, alcohol, laundry, gifts and internet. In the event of an early descent from the mountain, for any reason, the additional costs, such as hotel nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the climber.

content.value: A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Everyone who has stood on the summit of Aconcagua got there step by step, and mountain by mountain. If your previous mountain is already behind you and Aconcagua is next, we are here.
Frequently asked questions
How many days does it take to climb Aconcagua?

On the HighAir expedition the whole journey lasts 20 days, about 17 of them inside the park. The itinerary includes acclimatization and rest days, three high camps and two buffer days for bad weather. That time is what allows the body to acclimatize and the expedition to wait for a good weather window.
Do I need technical climbing experience for Aconcagua?

No. The Normal Route, which we climb, is not a technical route and involves no roped climbing, but when there is snow or ice on the upper mountain you walk in crampons. What you do need is previous experience at an altitude of at least 5,000 m, such as Kilimanjaro or the Everest Base Camp trek, good fitness and warm, quality gear.
How much is the Aconcagua climbing permit?

The price is set anew every season. In the 2025/26 season a foreign climber on the Horcones route with an authorized company paid 1,170 US dollars, and in the early sale for the 2026/27 season the permit was offered at 950 dollars. The permit is not included in the price of our expedition, and we help you obtain it.
When is the season for climbing Aconcagua?
The climbing season is the southern hemisphere summer, roughly from early December to early March. Our expeditions depart between December and February.
Do I need a visa for Argentina?

Citizens of the US, Canada, the UK, the EU and most of Latin America enter Argentina without a visa for a tourist stay. Check the validity of your passport and the current entry rules for your nationality before you fly.
What language do the guides speak?
The climb is led by professional local guides who speak English and Spanish and have long experience leading groups on the mountain.
